title: Talking About Ongoing Actions with Present Perfect Continuous
summary: You will learn how to use the present perfect continuous tense. This helps you talk about actions that started in the past and are still happening now.

sections.p: To form the present perfect continuous, use 'have' or 'has' plus 'been' and the main verb with '-ing'. Use 'have been' with I, you, we, and they. Use 'has been' with he, she, and it. This structure connects a past action directly to the present moment.

ex.en: I have been waiting for the bus for twenty minutes.
ex.mean: I started waiting in the past and I am still waiting now.

ex.en: She has been studying English all morning.
ex.mean: Her studying started earlier today and continues now.

ex.en: We have been living in this city for five years.
ex.mean: Our living here started five years ago and is still happening.

sections.p: We often use 'for' and 'since' with this tense. Use 'for' to talk about a duration of time, like 'for two hours' or 'for a long time'. Use 'since' to show the exact starting point of the action, such as 'since Monday' or 'since 2010'.

ex.en: He has been working here for six months.
ex.mean: Six months is the total length of time.

ex.en: They have been playing tennis since three o'clock.
ex.mean: Three o'clock is the exact time the game started.

sections.p: We use the present perfect continuous when we want to show that an activity is important, ongoing, or maybe even a little tiring. Sometimes you can see the physical result of the action in the present, like being tired or having wet clothes from rain.

ex.en: You look tired. Have you been working hard?
ex.mean: I see you are tired and I think you worked for a long time.

ex.en: It has been raining all day.
ex.mean: The rain started earlier and is still falling right now.

tip: Remember the formula: subject + have/has + been + verb-ing. Think of it as a bridge connecting past time to the present moment.
